<reason>A better justified the distinction between operational safeguards and reputation-only exclusion, while directly acknowledging that its rule could impose costs. Its gateway-access argument explained why coordinated reputational hostility could seriously harm compliant creators despite nominal alternatives. B offered a substantial brand-autonomy objection, especially for app stores, but relied too heavily on ownership and freedom of contract as complete answers to those harms. A also successfully distinguished access from promotion and rebutted the claim that merchants would lose their freedom to leave. B remained competitive but supplied less persuasive comparative weighing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s answer to the cost pressure was strongest: it accepted losses, preserved refusal for actual inability to settle payments, and clarified that other merchants remained free to depart. This weakened B’s framing of the proposal as either empty moral suasion or a creator veto over third-party choices.</best_rebuttal>
